transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Welcome to Signal & Noise. I'm Rachel Kim, and today is myth-busting day: the tech and media 'facts' everyone repeats at dinner parties. With me are tech reporter Omar Haddad and cognitive scientist Dr. Nina Alvarez.

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: Thanks Rachel. I've got a whole folder of things my relatives forward me, so this is therapy.

transcript.speaker: Nina
transcript.text: And I'm here to defend the human brain from the internet.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Let's start with streaming. Omar, how big is Netflix these days, really?

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: Huge. Netflix finished 2024 with just over 300 million paid memberships worldwide, and that was the last full-year count before they stopped publishing subscriber numbers.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: And music? It feels like everyone is on Spotify.

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: Spotify has about 400 million monthly active users, which is basically everyone with a smartphone in the West.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Okay, social. Is Facebook dying? My teenagers say it's dead.

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: Not even close. Facebook still has around 2 billion monthly users. People just don't post as much as they used to.

transcript.speaker: Nina
transcript.text: Which I'd argue is healthier for everyone, honestly.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Nina, your turn. What's the myth that annoys you most?

transcript.speaker: Nina
transcript.text: The idea that we only use ten percent of our brains. It's completely false: brain imaging shows activity across virtually the whole brain over the course of a normal day.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: So that movie lied to me. Great.

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: Speaking of attention, though, the average human attention span is now eight seconds, shorter than a goldfish's. Microsoft research found that, and it's why every clip we post has to be tiny.

transcript.speaker: Nina
transcript.text: Whatever the exact number, every app on your phone is designed to win those seconds. That part I'll happily believe.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Quick-fire tech history round. Omar, when did the iPhone come out?

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: The first iPhone went on sale in June 2007. Steve Jobs had unveiled it that January.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: And YouTube?

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: Google bought YouTube in 2006 for $1.65 billion, and people thought that was a crazy price at the time.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: And the web itself?

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: The web is younger than people think. Tim Berners-Lee invented it at CERN in 1999.

transcript.speaker: Nina
transcript.text: That makes me feel very old and very young at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Last one for this round. Twitter is X now. When did that happen?

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: Elon Musk rebranded Twitter as X in July 2023, and in my opinion the brand has never recovered.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Omar, you came up in print journalism. What did that collapse look like from the inside?

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: At the regional paper where I worked in 2009, our print ad revenue fell by half in a single year. We lost a third of the newsroom by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: Nina
transcript.text: That's brutal. And I suspect it's not over for a lot of outlets.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: Predictions, then. Where is all of this headed?

transcript.speaker: Nina
transcript.text: By 2030, more than half of everything posted online will be generated by AI. I'd bet money on it.

transcript.speaker: Omar
transcript.text: I think long-form audio is the most trustworthy medium we've got, because you can hear when someone is bluffing.

transcript.speaker: Rachel
transcript.text: On that note, thank you Omar and Nina. And listeners: check before you forward. See you next week on Signal & Noise.
